source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal & Selman (2010) On Adversarial Search Spaces and Sampling-Based Planning (ICAPS)
finding: Defines a level-k search trap: a move after which the opponent has a forced win in k moves. Shows such shallow traps are common in Chess, even in grandmaster games, but rare in Go until late.
numbers: Chess boards with a trap at level 1 to 7: about 7-10% of semi-random games at 31 ply, up to 15% at 47 ply; about 12% of 200 grandmaster games at 47 ply.
quote: UCT-style algorithms have a good chance of missing even very shallow traps and thus losing the game.
limits: Chess only; levels 1,3,5,7; semi-random games use a GNU Chess heuristic with prob 2/3 and random moves with prob 1/3.
agent_relevance: Traps exist where a loss hangs on a small part of the state. Agent tasks with a single fatal step (a deletion, a wrong final answer) are trap-like; averaging search is the wrong tool there.

source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal & Selman (2010) On Adversarial Search Spaces and Sampling-Based Planning (ICAPS)
finding: UCT gives the trap move almost the same value as the best move when the trap is at level 5 or 7. It spots only the level-3 trap.
numbers: UCT value of trap move vs UCT's best move (scale -1 to 1, ideal trap value -1): level-3 board -0.250 vs -0.083 (best by minimax -0.092); level-5 -0.012 vs +0.020; level-7 +0.004 vs +0.011.
limits: Four hand-picked boards, one per trap level (a level-1 board is also mentioned); UCT exploration constant 0.4; random playouts; single boards, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Averaged rollouts hide a forced loss. A scaffold must not trust a mean score where a worst-case check (a counterexample search) is cheap.

source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal & Selman (2010) On Adversarial Search Spaces and Sampling-Based Planning (ICAPS)
finding: More samples did not fix it. Even at 10 times the nodes minimax needs to find the trap, UCT's value for a level-5 or deeper trap stayed high, and UCT searched far deeper than needed.
numbers: With 10x the minimax node count, UCT trap value stays above -0.15 for level-5 and level-7 traps; only the level-3 trap value drops. Wasted search depth grows about exponentially with trap depth.
limits: Single-board demonstration; not a win-rate comparison.
agent_relevance: More rollouts is not a cure for missed traps. Add a different kind of check, not more of the same sampling.

source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal & Selman (2010) Understanding Sampling Style Adversarial Search Methods (UAI)
finding: With no Chess knowledge, UCT beats fixed-depth minimax. Soft traps (a move that hands the opponent a large gain, not a forced win) are common in grandmaster games.
numbers: 52% of 50 grandmaster games had at least one soft trap (MM-8 and MM-2 disagreed strongly on the best move). MM-6-R beat MM-2-R 66% of the time. UCT with a heuristic (UCT-H) beat a 10,000-iteration random-playout UCT in 55.0%, 85.5% and 96.5% of games with only 50, 100 and 1,000 iterations.
limits: Chess, GNU Chess modified to be knowledge-free; the UCT-vs-minimax table cells did not extract cleanly, so only the text-stated figures are quoted.
agent_relevance: UCT is not weak in general. It is strong when no trap sits within the horizon. The limit is trap density, a property of the task.

source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal & Selman (2010) Understanding Sampling Style Adversarial Search Methods (UAI)
finding: Synthetic binary trees of depth 20: when early samples mislead (a decoy subtree averages 0.5 vs 0 for the true winning side), UCT needs much longer to turn away. The delay is largest when the winning line is shallow or the opponent's refutation is deep.
numbers: Trees of depth 20 with planted critical nodes; a table of convergence-time effects by strategy depth (shallow, mid-level, deep) is reported; the percentages fall from 33%-40% in the shallow row to 0.2%-16% in the deep row.
limits: Synthetic trees only. Column labels of the table were lost in the text extract, so read the numbers as a trend, not as exact conditions.
agent_relevance: A misleading early reward signal (a plausible but wrong first step) costs many iterations. Early estimates in an LLM tree are noisy, so expect the same lock-in.

source: Ramanujan & Selman (2011) Trade-Offs in Sampling-Based Adversarial Planning (ICAPS)
finding: In Mancala, a game where minimax also works, UCT with tuned exploration beats MM-8 with a heuristic, so UCT is not intrinsically weak. A variant that backs up max values (UCTMAXH) beats plain averaging.
numbers: Best exploration constant c = 2.5; c = 20 gives a regular, minimax-like tree; small c gives an unfocused tree and weak play. Several hundred games per point.
quote: an algorithm that performs unsafe pruning outperforms a full-width search
limits: Mancala (6 pits, 4 stones, plus an 8-pit, 6-stone board); win rates read from plots.
agent_relevance: Exploration setting has a clear optimum per domain. The width/exploration setting in our scaffold must be fixed by a pilot, not guessed.

source: Ramanujan & Selman (2011) Trade-Offs in Sampling-Based Adversarial Planning (ICAPS)
finding: Tests the trap explanation directly. With terminal nodes hidden (partial games), UCT does better against minimax than in full games. Once terminal nodes come into view, minimax catches up.
numbers: UCTMAXH win rate against MM-k on partial games is above its complete-game win rate; the win rate drops as lookahead k grows because terminal nodes then become visible to minimax.
limits: Mancala only; consistent with the trap hypothesis but a single domain; read from plots.
agent_relevance: Supports a domain-dependent view: MCTS suits 'build a positional edge', and is weak for 'avoid a sudden fatal move'.

source: Baier & Winands (2018) MCTS-Minimax Hybrids with State Evaluations (JAIR 62)
finding: Embedding a shallow minimax search in MCTS repairs trap weakness. Node priors from enhanced minimax (MCTS-IP-M-k) is the best hybrid in Othello, Breakthrough and Catch the Lion. But plain alpha-beta still wins in two of three games.
numbers: Hybrid vs enhanced alpha-beta, 1000 games each: wins 66.9% in Breakthrough, 17.4% in Catch the Lion, 26.9% in Othello.
quote: MCTS is still more susceptible to traps than alpha-beta
limits: Board games with heuristic evaluations; the alpha-beta baseline was tuned against the hybrids; Catch the Lion is the most tactical game.
agent_relevance: Even the best fix leaves tactical games to full-width checks. Our program should run exhaustive checks on short horizons and use sampling only for long horizons.

source: Baier & Winands (2018) MCTS-Minimax Hybrids with State Evaluations (JAIR 62)
finding: Independent confirmation that trap density predicts how much minimax helps MCTS: all hybrids gain most in Catch the Lion, which has many shallow hard traps.
numbers: Informed rollouts (MCTS-IR-E) vs baseline MCTS-Solver with random rollouts: win rate 79.9% in Othello, 75.4% in Breakthrough, 96.8% in Catch the Lion (2000 games each, p<0.001). Depth-1 minimax in rollouts (MCTS-IR-M): 73.9%, 65.7%, 96.5%. In Breakthrough the stronger move ordering raised the k-best hybrid's win rate vs MCTS-IP-E from 49.6% to 77.8%.
limits: The authors say the Othello result (minimax stronger than expected) is not fully explained; they suggest soft traps. Different games differ in more than trap density.
agent_relevance: Gains from a cheap local lookahead are largest where one wrong move ends the game. Use a lookahead check at operators that can be fatal.

source: Coquelin & Munos (2007) Bandit Algorithms for Tree Search (UAI)
finding: Proof that UCT can be badly over-optimistic. In a constructed tree it needs hyper-exponential time in depth D before it finds the best branch, far worse than uniform search.
numbers: For D = 20, the transition phase lasts about 10^156837 trials with the sqrt-type confidence sequence (double exponential in D). With the standard logarithmic bound the regret is a tower of D-1 exponentials.
quote: UCT is over-optimistic in some sense, leading to a worst-case regret that may be very poor
limits: Worst-case construction with deterministic rewards where good branches look bad early; real trees are usually kinder. The paper also proposes safer variants (BAST, exponential-scale confidence).
agent_relevance: Worst case, not typical. It still shows that sample means can hide a good branch for a very long time. Keep a width-first fallback so search cannot sink all budget in one misleading branch.

source: Orseau, Lelis, Lattimore & Weber (2018) Single-Agent Policy Tree Search With Guarantees (NeurIPS)
finding: For deterministic single-agent puzzles with sparse reward, MCTS reverts to near-uniform search. A policy-guided best-first search (LevinTS) with a node-expansion bound solves all test levels.
numbers: 1,000 generated Sokoban levels: Uniform search solves 88; LubyTS(512,32) solves 884 +/- 4; LevinTS solves 1,000 (avg plan length 39.8, 6.6M expansions); LAMA planner solves 1,000 (3.15M expansions).
quote: if the reward is very sparse--for example the agent is rewarded only at the end of the task--MCTS algorithms revert to uniform search
limits: The baselines are uniform and sampling searches, not UCT run directly; the policy comes from an A3C network; Sokoban only.
agent_relevance: For single-agent tasks with one goal and no dense reward, a policy-guided best-first search with a budget bound beats sampling search. This matches the schema's checked, budgeted steps.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs (ICML)
finding: A KataGo-style system with MCTS at superhuman strength has a blind spot. Adversarial policies exploit it without playing Go well.
numbers: >97% win rate vs KataGo at superhuman settings; >99% vs no-search KataGo; cyclic adversary 95.7% over 1,052 games vs Latest(def) at 4,096 visits; 72% at 10^7 visits; trained with under 14% of KataGo's compute. The adversaries lose to amateurs.
quote: Our adversaries do not win by playing Go well. Instead, they trick KataGo into making serious blunders
limits: Needs gray-box access to the victim network; win rate falls as victim visits rise but stays above 50% at 10 million nodes. Tromp-Taylor rules.
agent_relevance: More search did not remove a systematic blind spot. A learned evaluator that is wrong in one pattern stays wrong at every depth; an outside check is needed.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs (ICML)
finding: The exploit transfers to other Go AIs and humans can copy it, so the flaw lies in what search plus network misjudge, not in one network's quirk.
numbers: Pass-adversary wins 99.9% vs no-search Latest with 600 visits. The cyclic attack transfers zero-shot to other superhuman Go AIs. Human experts used it to beat several superhuman AIs.
limits: Transfer shown on a small set of open Go AIs; no claim outside Go.
agent_relevance: A flaw that humans can learn means a separate human-readable rule check could catch it. Support external probes of the final answer.

source: Tseng, McLean, Pelrine, Wang & Gleave (2024) Can Go AIs Be Adversarially Robust? (AAAI 2025)
finding: Three natural fixes (adversarial training on hand-built positions, iterated adversarial training, a different network architecture) block old attacks but not newly trained ones. Cyclic attacks remain.
numbers: A cyclic-attack variant beats the defended agent 90% of the time with 26% of the defense compute; another wins 81% with 5%; gift-adversary wins 91% vs dec23-victim at 512 visits; a continuous adversary wins 65%; big-adversary 56%.
limits: Win rates fall as the victim searches more, and some attacks lose efficacy at higher visits. One game, one engine family.
agent_relevance: Patching one failure leaves the class of failures. Do not call a verification layer complete after one patch; keep re-attacking it.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS, NeurIPS)
finding: Under equal generation budgets, plain MCTS with an LLM does not beat repeated sampling on abstract reasoning (ARC-AGI) and is mixed on coding.
numbers: Budget 128 generations, mean +/- sd. ARC-AGI Pass@2: repeated sampling 15.0 (GPT-4o) and 18.6 (DeepSeek-V3); standard MCTS 9.0 and 14.0; AB-MCTS-M 12.3 and 16.0. LiveCodeBench: repeated sampling 37.8/40.7, standard MCTS 36.7/43.2. CodeContest: 37.9/43.2 vs 37.5/43.8. Average rank: repeated sampling 3.5, standard MCTS 4.2, AB-MCTS-M 2.3.
quote: repeated sampling proves to be a strong baseline in our setup
limits: Coding differences are within the noise. The authors' own adaptive method wins on average but still loses to repeated sampling on ARC-AGI. Uses an external feedback score.
agent_relevance: On tasks where a candidate can be fully checked, wide sampling is a hard baseline. Report sampling-only controls before adding a tree.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS, NeurIPS)
finding: LLM trees have unbounded width, but standard MCTS must fix a branching number. Making the width adaptive recovers gains.
numbers: ARC-AGI with DeepSeek-V3, budget up to 512 generations: repeated sampling begins to plateau while standard MCTS and AB-MCTS keep improving. On CodeContest AB-MCTS leads from budget 32 up.
limits: The authors' own method, so possible tuning bias; curves are moving averages.
agent_relevance: The width/depth split decides the result. Put it under the budget governor, not fixed.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cost-Awareness in Tree-Search LLM Planning: A Systematic Study
finding: LLM tree planners find feasible plans more often than chain-of-thought but get much worse with plan length, and extra node expansions do not buy optimal plans.
numbers: TIGHT cost budget, success rate for plan length L=2,4,6,8,10,12: MCTS 1.00, 0.92, 0.50, 0.11, 0.05, 0.00 (avg 0.43); Bi-Search avg 0.45; ToT-BFS 0.17; CoT with Claude 0.36. LOOSE budget: MCTS avg 0.61 (1.00, 1.00, 0.86, 0.55, 0.20, 0.05), Bi-Search 1.00, CoT Claude 0.54. Cap of 500 node expansions.
quote: additional search computation does not reliably improve optimality
limits: Planning with unequal action costs; LLM scores guide node choice. The table block labels were partly lost in extraction, so only TIGHT and LOOSE are quoted.
agent_relevance: Long chains of dependent steps break tree search quickly. Keep chains short and checked at each step.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cost-Awareness in Tree-Search LLM Planning: A Systematic Study
finding: MCTS beats ToT on feasibility, but at long horizons it no longer beats a strong non-search LLM. Bidirectional search does better than MCTS.
numbers: At L=8,10,12 optimality of tree methods falls and does not pass CoT with Claude; LOOSE success at L=12: MCTS 0.05, Bi-Search 1.00. MCTS keeps improving with more expansions but shows diminishing returns.
limits: Single study; a domain with a known goal state favours backward search.
agent_relevance: Where the goal is known, search backward from it (means-ends style) as well as forward.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor & Narayanan (2024, rev. 2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: Scaling search by resampling against an imperfect verifier has a ceiling. False positives that pass the check cannot be reduced by more samples, and the false-positive rate rises with weaker models.
numbers: Tested on HumanEval+ (200 samples per task and model; 1,000 for Command Light) and MBPP+ (50 per task), using the weaker original tests as verifier. Optimal number of attempts is often fewer than 10 and can be zero for weak models.
quote: Resampling cannot decrease this probability, so it imposes an upper bound to the accuracy
limits: Code with unit tests as verifier; applies to any search whose value signal has a false-positive rate.
agent_relevance: The verifier must be as strong as the claim. A search over a weak check selects answers that fool it; cap attempts and keep a held-out check.

source: Zhang et al. (Qwen team, 2025) The Lessons of Developing Process Reward Models in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: The value signal behind step-level tree search is often learned from Monte Carlo rollouts, and it is noisy: a wrong step can lead to a right answer and the reverse. PRMs trained this way did worse than ones trained on LLM-judge or human labels.
numbers: Authors report MC-estimation PRMs gave significantly worse performance and generalization than LLM-as-judge and human labels. Policy Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct, 8 samples per query on GSM8K, MATH, OlympiadBench, Omni-MATH; many correct-answer responses had flawed steps, more often on harder sets.
quote: MC estimation relies on completion models, which can generate correct answers from incorrect steps
limits: Math domain; manual annotation of a sample; Best-of-N scoring is partly inflated by correct-answer but flawed-process outputs.
agent_relevance: A tree search is only as good as its value estimate. Do not select steps by rollout value without checking it against labels.

source: Chen et al. (2025) From Mathematical Reasoning to Code: Generalization of Process Reward Models in Test-Time Scaling
finding: With a PRM, MCTS beat beam search, best-of-N and majority vote as the generation budget grew, and majority vote came last. A counter-result to the 'sampling wins' findings.
numbers: Reported order as budget rises: MCTS > beam search > best-of-N > majority vote. Table row, four columns of code scores: majority vote (4 samples) 86.8, 76.0, 40.1, 54.6; PRM-Math 89.6, 76.2, 41.9, 54.2. A PRM trained on code showed no clear edge over the math PRM.
limits: Needs a trained PRM and time; MCTS is slower per answer; best-of-N favoured at small budgets; ordering read from plots.
agent_relevance: Search wins when a trained, domain-matched value model exists and the budget is large. We have neither, so default to sampling plus checks.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling: Efficiency Limits and Linguistic Signals
finding: Without a trained verifier, simple majority voting beats sequential revision and mixture-of-agents on reasoning models. Non-reasoning models hit a 'reasoning floor' that more compute does not lift.
numbers: Consistent ordering across tasks; general-purpose models fail to match reasoning-optimised ones even with about ten times more inference compute. Correct answers are shorter and use fewer hedging markers.
quote: simple majority voting consistently outperforms sophisticated sequential revision and mixture-of-agents frameworks
limits: Verifier-free setting on hard tasks (PhD experts reach only about 65% on one); tree search was not the main method tested.
agent_relevance: No-verifier baseline: majority vote. A search scheme must beat it at matched tokens to be kept.

source: Qian et al. (2026) PAC-CF: Calibrating Irreversible Frontier Pruning in LLM-Guided Search
finding: Pruning branches by LLM-evaluator score is irreversible, and the evaluator's errors are systematic, so repeated scoring does not remove them. A calibrated gap threshold set on held-out tasks keeps a valid branch with a coverage guarantee.
numbers: Five controllers (UCT-MCTS, ToolChain*, LATS, ToolTree, LevinTS), three domains, budgets B100 to B500. Observed task coverage: 97.00% for UCT-MCTS (97/100), 95.88% for ToolChain*. ToolTree utility +4.38 points; physical requests down about 18.9% and tokens down about 23.6% on the natural-termination cohort.
quote: systematic ranking errors can persist under repeated scoring and remove useful branches
limits: Preprint (v6, Oct 2026); authors' own method; the guarantee needs exchangeable tasks and verifier labels after search.
agent_relevance: Pruning needs calibration on held-out tasks. Do not prune on an uncalibrated score.

source: Ramanujan et al. (2010-11) and Baier & Winands (2018), synthesis of the rival explanations for MCTS weakness
finding: Two rival explanations for where MCTS fails: (1) trap density (selective sampling and averaging miss short forced losses); (2) weak value estimates from random playouts. Evidence so far favours (1) for Chess-like games, with AlphaZero-style learned evaluators narrowing the gap but not closing it.
numbers: Baier & Winands: gains from minimax were largest in Catch the Lion (many shallow traps) and smallest in Breakthrough. Ramanujan: 12-15% of Chess positions at 47 ply hold a shallow trap.
limits: Only a few games; no study measures trap density in agent or language tasks.
agent_relevance: Open question: how trap-dense are our tasks? A pilot could count single-step fatal errors in our traces before choosing a search style.

source: Orseau, Lelis, Lattimore & Weber (2018) Single-Agent Policy Tree Search With Guarantees (NeurIPS)
finding: Sampling-based policy search degrades when its sample count per restart is small, while an enumeration with a proven expansion bound does not. More restarts and longer rollouts help, with cost.
numbers: Solved of 1,000 Sokoban levels (5 seeds): LubyTS(256,1) 753 +/- 5; LubyTS(256,32) 870 +/- 2; LubyTS(512,32) 884 +/- 4; MultiTS(1,200) 669 +/- 5; MultiTS(200,200) 881 +/- 1. Expansions rise from about 0.6M (LubyTS 256,1; extract printed 63,8481) to 11.5M for LubyTS(512,32).
limits: Parameter-heavy: results depend on two sampling parameters; table cell for one row was garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Sampling search has many parameters that decide the result; the deterministic bounded search has none to tune. Prefer the version with fewer knobs.
